meta.tagline: Capital of the South: civil rights legacy, peach trees and soul food tables

overview.title: Welcome to Atlanta
overview.intro: Atlanta is a forest city with skyscrapers: its tree canopy is a record-holder among big American cities, and the highways flow through the green. But the city's real story is written in its streets — Martin Luther King was born here, the civil rights movement marched from here, and Sweet Auburn Avenue carries that struggle's memory. Today's Atlanta jogs along the BeltLine, a railway loop turned park, meets over a plate of lemon pepper wings, feeds off the world's busiest airport and smiles as it says 'y'all'. Southern hospitality here is not a cliché but the daily language.

local_word.definition: The contraction of 'you all': the official pronoun of the South. It solves the singular-plural problem in one word and warms every sentence. When you hear 'y'all come back now', know the door is always open. The moment you start using it, Atlanta promotes you from guest to neighbor.

rules.title: Read Atlanta through its neighborhoods
rules.description: Downtown is the showcase; the neighborhoods are the soul: Old Fourth Ward's BeltLine, Virginia-Highland's porch-front houses and Decatur's square feel like separate cities. Pick one or two districts a day and connect them wisely — those who love Atlanta love it neighborhood by neighborhood.

rules.title: Plan against the traffic hours
rules.description: Atlanta traffic is legendary: stay off the highways from 07:00–09:30 and 16:00–19:00. The MARTA train saves lives on the airport–Midtown line; a car covers the rest, but hour choice is everything — at midday the city shrinks by half.

rules.title: Give the civil rights legacy its time
rules.description: The MLK National Historical Park is free: his birth home, the Ebenezer church where he preached, and his tomb fit into one walk. Combine it with the National Center for Civil and Human Rights — understanding Atlanta begins with this legacy; the rest arrives as food and music.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: World's busiest · 20 min to town by MARTA

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: Civil rights trail and the park loop

quick_facts.label: Language
quick_facts.sub: The Southern accent is sweet and warm

tip.label: The Atlanta philosophy
tip.text: Hurry violates Southern manners: breakfast runs long, conversation runs sweet, and the sweet tea comes in a big glass. Keep the schedule loose — Atlanta's best moments hide in porch conversations and BeltLine walks.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Atlanta is a car city, but the MARTA train, the BeltLine and smart hour choices do a visitor's work.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: From Hartsfield-Jackson, MARTA's red/gold line reaches Downtown and Midtown in 20 minutes: cheap, painless, traffic-free. Inside the world's busiest airport the inter-terminal distances are serious — budget your transfer generously.

items.title: The MARTA train
items.description: Four lines weave the airport, Downtown, Midtown and Decatur: ride with a Breeze card. Coverage is limited, but for anything on the line it's the smartest choice — and on game and concert days it always beats the car.

items.title: Walking the BeltLine
items.description: The old railway loop became a park-path: the Eastside Trail walks you from Old Fourth Ward to Ponce City Market among artworks. Walk, run or rent a bike — this is Atlanta's most delightful 'transit line'.

items.title: Uber/Lyft and a car
items.description: Ride apps are the practical bridge between neighborhoods; renting a car adds freedom on longer stays. Parking is mostly easy and paid — prices soar on stadium days, so move early.

items.title: The streetcar and themed routes
items.description: The Downtown streetcar loops out to Sweet Auburn: a practical link to the MLK district. Tour Atlanta by theme: one day for the civil rights trail, one for the BeltLine neighborhoods — the city makes sense through its themes.

callout.label: BeltLine tip
callout.text: On Saturday morning enter the Eastside Trail from the Old Fourth Ward end: walk to Ponce City Market among joggers, street art and coffee carts. Ride the rooftop amusement park or settle into the food hall for lunch — this is the classic opening of an Atlanta weekend.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Atlanta the choice is a matter of the loop: city life turns inside the Perimeter — Midtown's walkability, O4W's BeltLine rhythm, Decatur's square-town calm.

local_word.definition: 'Inside the Perimeter / Outside the Perimeter': life divided by the I-285 ring road that circles the city. ITP means city rhythm, OTP means suburban calm — Atlantans define their identity with these letters. For a visitor the rule is simple: stay ITP, tour ITP.

items.name: Midtown
items.description: Piedmont Park, the art museum and the MARTA line together: Atlanta's most walkable district. Dense with restaurants and bars — the most practical base for a first visit.

items.name: Old Fourth Ward
items.description: MLK's neighborhood now lives the city's liveliest transformation: the BeltLine, Ponce City Market and historic streets interwoven. For history and new Atlanta at one address.

items.name: Virginia-Highland
items.description: Bungalow houses, neighborhood bars and independent shops: Atlanta's leafy, front-porch daily life. A short drive to the center — the calm, characterful side.

items.name: Downtown
items.description: The aquarium, Centennial Park and the convention hotels: walking distance to the big sights. It quiets down at night — for the sight-packed, practically-located stay.

items.name: Decatur
items.description: An old town connected by MARTA: its square, independent restaurants and bookshop run on their own rhythm. For sleeping in a town while staying tied to the city.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Atlanta's calendar is built on spring blossoms and autumn coolness; summer is humid and stormy, winter short and mild.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Dogwood Spring
items.subtitle: Spring · Blossoming neighborhoods, pollen-yellow cars
items.description: In late March the city bursts into bloom: dogwoods and azaleas turn the neighborhoods pastel and Piedmont Park fills with festivals. In pollen weeks the cars turn yellow — come prepared if you have allergies; the scenery is worth it.

callout.label: April tip
callout.text: In mid-April the Dogwood Festival turns Piedmont Park into an art market: open the day with a BeltLine walk. For a blossom tour, the streets of Virginia-Highland and Druid Hills are the most generous route.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Humid Southern Summer
items.subtitle: Summer · Hot humid days, afternoon thunder
items.description: Summer Atlanta is humid and thunder-prone: the midday heat is heavy and the afternoon storm arrives short and loud. Early mornings and evenings outdoors, middays in museums and the aquarium — iced sweet tea is this season's official drink.

callout.label: Midday note
callout.text: Don't force the BeltLine's shadeless stretches at summer noon: set the walk before 09:00 or in the late afternoon. The afternoon storm forbids picnic plans made without a radar check — flexibility is the key to an Atlanta summer.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Golden Southern Fall
items.subtitle: Autumn · Cool evenings, football Saturdays
items.description: October breaks the humidity, the tree canopy turns gold, and porch season opens: these are Atlanta's finest weeks. On Saturdays college football takes the city — factor in stadium-day traffic and hotel prices.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: In late October the historic gardens of Oakland Cemetery are fall color's most graceful stage: look up the guided evening tours. Afterwards, porch coffee in the Grant Park neighborhood — the exact formula of a Southern autumn.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Mild and Quiet
items.subtitle: Winter · Brief cold snaps, museum and table season
items.description: Atlanta winter is soft: snow is rare, and when it falls the city panics comically. Museums, the aquarium and soul food tables are the season's natural program — hotels run calm and prices friendly.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: Come around MLK Day: commemorations fill his birth neighborhood and special programs fill Ebenezer. Walking the civil rights trail in that atmosphere is the experience closest to Atlanta's heart.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The Atlanta table is the capital of Southern cooking: the crunch of fried chicken, the warmth of soul food, and the city's own pride in lemon pepper.

local_word.definition: The South's lunchroom order: choose one meat and three sides — and mac and cheese counts as a vegetable here. This tray-line table is the everyday form of the soul food tradition. If collard greens, candied yams and cornbread made it onto the tray, you're in the right place.

items.name: Lemon pepper wings
items.description: Atlanta's signature wing: dusted with lemon pepper, or 'wet' with butter sauce if you dare. An institution of the city's wing halls, woven into rap culture — stock up on wet wipes.
items.tag: The city's signature · try it wet

items.name: Meat-and-three soul food
items.description: Fried chicken or stewed meat with collard greens, mac and cheese and cornbread: the tray-line Southern classic. Join the lunch queue at the storied halls of Sweet Auburn and the Westside.

items.name: The Buford Highway table
items.description: The city's northeast corridor is a boulevard of world cooking: Vietnamese pho, Korean barbecue and Mexican taquerías side by side. Give it one evening — Atlanta's least-known superpower.
items.tag: World corridor · give it a night

items.name: Chicken and waffles brunch
items.description: Crisp chicken, hot waffle and maple syrup: the sweet-savory summit of the Southern brunch. Sharing tables with the Sunday church crowd is among the city's truest hours.

items.name: Peach cobbler and sweet tea
items.description: Georgia peaches baked in syrup, beside a giant glass of iced sweet tea: the closing signature of the Southern table. A scoop of vanilla ice cream on the cobbler — a classic beyond negotiation.
items.tag: Georgia signature · ice cream on top

items.name: The drive-in chili dog
items.description: A century-old drive-in tradition: chili dogs with onion rings and a frosted fruit drink. Order to the cry of 'What'll ya have?' — Atlanta nostalgia in standing form.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: You don't need a tourist 'Southern' chain in Atlanta: the locals' queue, the after-church crowd and a handwritten daily menu point to the right address. Tipping 18–20% is standard — Southern sweetness is mutual at the register too.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the aquarium; these six are Atlanta's neighborhood-scale, story-laden hidden face.

items.name: Jackson Street Bridge
items.description: The bridge looking from Old Fourth Ward to the Downtown skyline: familiar from the 'Walking Dead' credits, it fills with photographers at sunset. Free, open and striking at every hour — bring the tripod.

items.name: Oakland Cemetery
items.description: A Victorian garden cemetery from 1850: magnolias, Margaret Mitchell's grave and a skyline view. Atlantans jog and picnic here — history itself is the park.

items.name: The Krog Street Tunnel
items.description: The tunnel linking Cabbagetown to Inman Park lives as a gallery of ever-changing graffiti layers: a different wall on every pass. A natural pause on the BeltLine walk.

items.name: Sweet Auburn Curb Market
items.description: The city market open since 1918: butchers, soul food stalls and new-generation kitchens under one roof. Pair it with the MLK district — lunch's most historic address.

items.name: Old Fourth Ward Park and its pond
items.description: An amphitheater park at the BeltLine's foot: the Ponce City Market tower reflects in the water. Sit on the grass at sunset — new Atlanta's postcard is taken from here.

items.name: The Ponce City Market rooftop
items.description: A mini amusement park, bar and city views atop the old Sears warehouse, with the food hall below. Play skee-ball, drink something against the skyline — Atlanta's most entertaining roof.

callout.label: Route strategy
callout.text: Most of these corners line up on one route: Jackson Street Bridge → O4W Park → BeltLine → Ponce City → Krog Tunnel → Oakland Cemetery. On foot, in one day — Atlanta's best day lives inside this loop.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Atlanta is an honest city; its traps grow from wrong expectations more than bad intent — know these four.

items.name: Mistaking Downtown for Atlanta
items.description: The icon district goes quiet at night; the tourist who stays only there leaves saying 'Atlanta had no soul' — but the city lives in its neighborhoods.
items.instead: Fit the icons into half a day and give the rest to O4W, Virginia-Highland, Decatur and Buford Highway. Atlanta's answer always lives in the question 'which neighborhood?'

items.name: Underestimating rush hour
items.description: The road navigation calls 20 minutes becomes 70 at 17:30: Atlanta traffic murders plans.
items.instead: Set cross-town moves in the 10:00–15:30 band; gather the evening program in one neighborhood. For anything on the MARTA line, take the train — on game days this rule turns golden.

items.name: The tourist 'Southern food' window
items.description: Some 'authentic Southern' restaurants near the icons sell a frozen-food cliché menu at high prices.
items.instead: Watch for the locals' lunch queue: meat-and-three halls, Sweet Auburn stalls and neighborhood brunches give twice the flavor for the same money. The smell of cast iron is a better guide than any sign.

items.name: Event-day parking games
items.description: On stadium and concert days some private lots run outrageous 'event pricing'; towing from unmarked areas is a real risk.
items.instead: Reserve a spot in advance with a parking app, or arrive by MARTA: station lots are cheap and safe. Read the street sign to its last line — Atlanta's tow trucks work fast.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Atlanta's formula is neighborhood + hour + table: go to the right district at the right time and sit at the locals' table. Smile and say 'y'all' — the Southern door opens from the inside.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the MLK legacy to the BeltLine rooftop

steps.title: Southern breakfast
steps.description: Open the day with biscuits, eggs and grits: the fuel station of a Southern morning. Large coffee — there's much walking today.

steps.title: MLK National Historical Park
steps.description: The birth home, Ebenezer Baptist Church and the tomb: walk the civil rights legacy in morning calm. The visitor center is free.

steps.title: Lunch at Sweet Auburn market
steps.description: Soul food at the century-old market stalls: take your tray and eat inside history.

steps.title: The BeltLine walk
steps.description: Enter the Eastside Trail from O4W Park: street art, joggers and the Krog Tunnel detour on the way to Ponce City Market.

steps.title: The Ponce City rooftop
steps.description: Snack in the food hall, then the mini amusement park and the view up top: Atlanta's transformation story in one building.

steps.title: Lemon pepper evening
steps.description: Lemon pepper wet at a wing hall, sweet tea alongside: close with the night skyline from Jackson Street Bridge.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Legacy, neighborhoods and a world table — the full Atlanta

steps.title: Classic Atlanta
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: the MLK park, Sweet Auburn, the BeltLine, Ponce City, a lemon pepper night.

steps.title: Icons and park day
steps.description: Whale sharks at the Georgia Aquarium in the morning (timed ticket); Centennial Park and the Center for Civil and Human Rights at noon; Piedmont Park + the Botanical Garden in the afternoon; a porch dinner in Virginia-Highland.

steps.title: Town square and the world corridor
steps.description: A morning walk in Oakland Cemetery's gardens; bookshop and lunch on the Decatur square; Fernbank or the High Museum in the afternoon; farewell dinner on Buford Highway — from pho to Korean barbecue.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Southern English is sweet music; these five phrases open doors and tables in Atlanta.

items.meaning: You all — the South's official pronoun; use it once and you're half local
The long form of hello — everyone asks it, from the register to the bus; you ask too
Tenderness or sweet needling, depending on context — the South's many-layered classic
Iced sweet tea — say 'tea' and it comes sweet anyway; in the South, this is tea
Atlanta's nickname — when you hear 'welcome to the A', you're home
